s0001.literal: The Grand Progenitor, High Emperor, taboo name Daocheng, style name Shaobo, surname Xiao, childhood taboo Doujiang, was the twenty-fourth-generation descendant of Xiao He, Chancellor of State of Han.
s0001.idiomatic: Emperor Gao, canonically titled Grand Progenitor, bore the name Daocheng and the style Shaobo; his clan was Xiao, and in childhood he was called Doujiang. He was the twenty-fourth in descent from Xiao He, Chancellor of State of Han.

s0002.literal: He's son Yan, Marquis of Ding of Zan, begot Palace Attendant Biao; Biao begot Grand Secretariat Aide Zhang; Zhang begot Hao; Hao begot Yang; Yang begot Censor-in-Chief Wangzhi; Wangzhi begot Household Minister Yu; Yu begot Imperial Secretary Shao; Shao begot Director of the Imperial Secretariat Hong; Hong begot Administrator of Jiyin Chan; Chan begot Administrator of Wu Commandery Yong; Yong begot Chancellor of Zhongshan Bao; Bao begot Erudite Zhou; Zhou begot Chief of Sheqiu Jiao; Jiao begot Provincial Attendant Kui; Kui begot Filial and Incorrupt Xiu; Xiu begot Aide of the Guangling Commandery Bao; Bao begot Grand Master of Palace Counsel Yi; Yi begot Magistrate of Huaiyin Zheng; Zheng begot Magistrate of Jiuqiu Jun; Jun begot Staff Officer for Assisting the State Yuezi, posthumously made Grand Minister of Ceremonies in the ninth month of the second year of Shengming of Song, who begot the Imperial Father.
s0002.idiomatic: Xiao He's son Yan, Marquis of Ding of Zan, fathered Palace Attendant Biao; from Biao the line ran through a grand secretariat aide named Zhang, then Hao, Yang, the censor-in-chief Wangzhi, the household minister Yu, the imperial secretary Shao, the director of the imperial secretariat Hong, the administrator of Jiyin Chan, the administrator of Wu Yong, the chancellor of Zhongshan Bao, the erudite Zhou, the chief of Sheqiu Jiao, the provincial attendant Kui, the filial and incorrupt Xiu, a Guangling commandery aide Bao, the grand master of palace counsel Yi, the magistrate of Huaiyin Zheng, the magistrate of Jiuqiu Jun, and the staff officer for assisting the state Yuezi—posthumously raised to Grand Minister of Ceremonies in the ninth month of Song's second Shengming year—who fathered the Imperial Father.

s0003.literal: Xiao He dwelt in Pei; Palace Attendant Biao, dismissed from office, dwelt in Zhongdu village, Zhongdu township, Lanling county, Donghai.
s0003.idiomatic: Xiao He had lived in Pei; after Palace Attendant Biao was dismissed, he settled in Zhongdu village, Zhongdu township, Lanling county in Donghai.

s0004.literal: In the first year of Yuankang of Jin, Donghai was divided to form Lanling commandery.
s0004.idiomatic: In Jin's first Yuankang year, Donghai was split off to form Lanling commandery.

s0005.literal: When the central dynasty fell into turmoil, Magistrate of Huaiyin Zheng, styled Gongqi, crossed the river and dwelt in the Eastern City ward of Wujin county, Jinling.
s0005.idiomatic: In the turmoil of the central court, Huaiyin's magistrate Zheng, styled Gongqi, crossed the Yangtze and settled in the Eastern City ward of Wujin in Jinling.

s0006.literal: Those dwelling east of the river all had their native lands registered in exile districts with the prefix "Southern" added; thus they became natives of Lanling in Southern Lanling.
s0006.idiomatic: Émigrés south of the Yangtze had their home districts registered in exile prefectures with "Southern" prefixed to the name; thus the clan became natives of Lanling in Southern Lanling.

s0007.literal: The Imperial Father taboo Chengzhi, style name Sibo.
s0007.idiomatic: The Imperial Father bore the name Chengzhi and the style Sibo.

s0008.literal: In youth he cherished great resolve; his talent and strength surpassed others; his clansmen, Administrator of Danyang Mu Zhi and Inspector of North Yanzhou Yuanzhi, both held him in esteem.
s0008.idiomatic: In youth he nursed great ambition, and his talent and force outstripped other men. His kinsmen Mu Zhi, administrator of Danyang, and Yuanzhi, inspector of North Yanzhou, both marked him for trust.

s0009.literal: At first he served as staff officer in the Establishing Might Office; in the Yixi era, when the Shu bandit Qiao Zong was first pacified, the Imperial Father was transferred to General Who Raises Martial Might and Administrator of the two commanderies of Angu and Wenshan, skilled at soothing and settling.
s0009.idiomatic: He first served on the staff of the Establishing Might office. In the Yixi era, when the Shu rebel Qiao Zong was newly subdued, the Imperial Father was made General Who Raises Martial Might and administrator of Angu and Wenshan, and proved adept at pacification.

s0010.literal: At the beginning of Yuanjia he was transferred to General Who Establishes Martial Glory and Administrator of Jinan.
s0010.idiomatic: Early in the Yuanjia reign he was transferred to General Who Establishes Martial Glory and made administrator of Jinan.

s0011.literal: In the seventh year, Right General Dao Yanzhi suffered great defeat on the northern campaign; the enemy took advantage of victory to break the commanderies and principalities of Qing Province; a separate commander, the Duke of Ping'an Yizhan Juan, raided Jinan; the Imperial Father led several hundred men to resist and drove them back.
s0011.idiomatic: In the seventh year, Right General Dao Yanzhi was routed on the northern expedition. The enemy pressed the victory, overrunning the commanderies of Qing, while a detached force under the Duke of Ping'an, Yizhan Juan, struck at Jinan. The Imperial Father led several hundred men to meet them and beat them back.

s0012.literal: The enemy masses gathered in strength; the Imperial Father had the troops lay down their arms and opened the city gates.
s0012.idiomatic: When the enemy host massed in strength, the Imperial Father ordered his men to stand down and opened the city gates.

s0013.literal: The crowd remonstrated, saying: "The bandits are many and we are few—why treat the enemy so lightly!"
s0013.idiomatic: His officers protested: "The enemy outnumber us—why show them such contempt?"

s0014.literal: The Imperial Father said: "Today we hang on defense in a desperate city; affairs are already critical; if we show weakness again, we shall surely be slaughtered—one must only meet them with a show of strength."
s0014.idiomatic: The Imperial Father said, "We cling to a doomed city on a hair trigger. If we show fear again, they will cut us down. We must meet them as though we were the stronger."

s0015.literal: The enemy suspected an ambush and therefore withdrew.
s0015.idiomatic: The enemy suspected a trap and drew off.

s0016.literal: Qing Province Inspector Xiao Sihua wished to abandon the prefecture and hold the defiles; the Imperial Father firmly remonstrated but was not obeyed; Sihua lost his footing and fled in rout.
s0016.idiomatic: Qing's inspector Xiao Sihua meant to abandon his seat and cling to mountain strongholds. The Imperial Father argued against it in vain; Sihua lost his footing and fled in rout.

s0017.literal: The next year, Grand General Who Conquers the South Tan Daoji turned from battle at Shouzhang and marched back; Huatai fell; Yanzhou Inspector Zhu Lingxiu was punished.
s0017.idiomatic: The following year Grand General Who Conquers the South Tan Daoji broke off fighting at Shouzhang and marched home; Huatai was lost, and Yanzhou's inspector Zhu Lingxiu was called to account.

s0018.literal: Emperor Wen of Song, because the Imperial Father had the merit of preserving the whole city, wrote in his own hand to the commander-in-chief, Prince of Changsha Yixin, saying: "Chengzhi in governing the people is straightforward and not behind in martial capacity; he is now proposed for Yanzhou—[lacuna] let Grand General Who Conquers the South Tan deliberate."
s0018.idiomatic: Emperor Wen of Song, crediting the Imperial Father with saving the city intact, wrote in his own hand to the commander-in-chief, Prince Yixin of Changsha: "Chengzhi governs with integrity and is no laggard in martial affairs. I propose him for Yanzhou—[text lost]—let Grand General Tan Daoji advise."

s0019.literal: The Imperial Father had no prior tie with Daoji; the matter therefore lapsed.
s0019.idiomatic: The Imperial Father had no old connection with Tan Daoji, and the appointment came to nothing.

s0020.literal: He was transferred to Central Corps Commander of the Assisting State and Pacifying North Army and to outer court gentleman.
s0020.idiomatic: He was transferred to central corps commander of the Assisting State and Pacifying North armies and to outer court gentleman.

s0021.literal: In the tenth year, Xiao Sihua became Inspector of Liang Province; the Imperial Father was his Wild Expansion Office marshal and Administrator of Hanzhong.
s0021.idiomatic: In the tenth year Xiao Sihua became inspector of Liang, and the Imperial Father served as his Wild Expansion army marshal and administrator of Hanzhong.

s0022.literal: The Di chieftain Yang Nandang raided Han River country; Liang Inspector Zhen Fahu abandoned the city and fled; Sihua reached Xiangyang but did not advance; the Imperial Father led a light column forward and attacked the Di puppet Administrator of Weixing Xue Jian at Golden Mountain, taking him.
s0022.idiomatic: The Di chieftain Yang Nandang raided the Han basin. Liang's inspector Zhen Fahu abandoned his city and fled; Sihua halted at Xiangyang and would not advance. The Imperial Father pushed ahead with a light column, attacked the Di puppet administrator of Weixing, Xue Jian, at Golden Mountain, and took him.

s0023.literal: Golden Mountain was an old garrison of Zhang Lu, south joining Han River country, north resting on the post road—of extreme strategic strength.
s0023.idiomatic: Golden Mountain had been Zhang Lu's old stronghold, joining the Han country to the south and commanding the post road to the north—ground of the utmost strength.

s0024.literal: When Jian had already been routed and scattered, the Imperial Father at once seized it.
s0024.idiomatic: Once Jian's force was broken, the Imperial Father seized the height at once.

s0025.literal: The Di puppet Inspectors of Liang and Qin, Zhao Wen, had first held the provincial city; hearing the Imperial Father had come, he withdrew to a lesser city; Xue Jian withdrew to encamp at Xiatao city and raised stockade camps; the Imperial Father led his army to face them across a distance of two li.
s0025.idiomatic: The Di puppet inspectors of Liang and Qin, Zhao Wen, already held the provincial seat; when he heard the Imperial Father was coming, he fell back to a lesser city. Xue Jian withdrew to Xiatao and threw up stockades. The Imperial Father drew up facing them two li away.

s0026.literal: Jian and the puppet Administrator of Fufeng Pu
s0026.idiomatic: Jian and the puppet administrator of Fufeng, Pu

s0028.literal: [Zao]zi exerted their full strength in battle; the Imperial Father inflicted a great defeat; Jian and the others shut their camps and dared not come out; Sihua followed after, and the bandits then gradually withdrew.
s0028.idiomatic: [Zao]'s son threw everything into the fight; the Imperial Father broke them utterly. Jian and his men shut themselves in camp and dared not stir; Sihua came up behind, and the enemy at last drew off.

s0029.literal: The Imperial Father advanced to Mount E'gong, was besieged for many days by the great host of Lü Ping, Left Guards General and Inspector of Shazhou; the Establishing Martial General Xiao Wangzhi, the Pacifying West staff commander Duan Jiu, and others arrived; attacking from within and without with combined force, they inflicted a great defeat.
s0029.idiomatic: The Imperial Father pushed on to Mount E'gong and was hemmed in for days by the great host of Lü Ping, Left Guards general and inspector of Shazhou. When the Establishing Martial general Xiao Wangzhi and the Pacifying West staff commander Duan Jiu came up, they struck from within and without and won a crushing victory.

s0030.literal: Nandang also sent his son He at the head of more than ten thousand foot and horse on both banks of the Han as reinforcements for Zhao Wen, pressing the attack on the Imperial Father.
s0030.idiomatic: Nandang also sent his son He with more than ten thousand foot and horse along both banks of the Han to reinforce Zhao Wen and press the Imperial Father.

s0031.literal: They faced one another for more than forty days.
s0031.idiomatic: The two sides stood off for more than forty days.

s0032.literal: The bandits all wore rhinoceros-hide armor; blades and arrows could not harm them.
s0032.idiomatic: The enemy all wore rhinoceros-hide armor against which blade and arrow could not bite.

s0033.literal: The Imperial Father ordered the army to cut spears several chi long and drive them in with great axes from behind; the bandits could not withstand it and therefore burned their camps and withdrew.
s0033.idiomatic: The Imperial Father ordered spears cut several chi long and driven home with great axes from behind; the enemy could not stand before them, burned their camps, and withdrew.

s0034.literal: The Imperial Father pursued to Nancheng; the mass of armies came up from behind and joined battle in succession, all victorious; Liang Province was pacified.
s0034.idiomatic: The Imperial Father pursued to Nancheng. The main columns came up from behind and fought in succession, winning every engagement, and Liang Province was pacified.

s0035.literal: An edict said: "Chengzhi received the mandate as vanguard, braved peril and went deep, repeatedly overcame with the whole army, and displayed loyal valor—he may be made General of Dragon Cavalry."
s0035.idiomatic: An edict declared: "Chengzhi, taking the mandate as vanguard, braved peril in deep country, and with the whole army won again and again, showing loyal valor—let him be made General of Dragon Cavalry."

s0036.literal: He followed the establishment in transfer to Pacifying the North army marshal; his post as administrator was unchanged.
s0036.idiomatic: He followed the establishment in transfer to marshal of the Pacifying North army while retaining his governorship.

s0037.literal: He entered the capital as Colonel of Rapid Cavalry for the Heir Apparent.
s0037.idiomatic: He entered the capital as Colonel of Rapid Cavalry on the heir apparent's staff.

s0038.literal: Emperor Wen, because of the merit in pacifying the Di, with Qingzhou vacant intended to appoint him.
s0038.idiomatic: Emperor Wen, honoring the Di campaign, meant to give him the vacant Qingzhou post.

s0039.literal: Prince of Pengcheng Yikang held the government; the Imperial Father would not attach himself to him; he was therefore transferred to central corps commander on the Prince of Jiangxia's staff as Grand Minister of Education, General of Dragon Cavalry, Administrator of South Taishan, enfeoffed as fifth-grade baron of Jinxing with a fief of three hundred forty households.
s0039.idiomatic: Prince Yikang of Pengcheng held the government, and the Imperial Father would not join his faction; he was therefore shifted to central corps commander on Prince Jiangxia's staff as grand minister of education, made General of Dragon Cavalry and administrator of South Taishan, and enfeoffed as fifth-rank baron of Jinxing with three hundred forty households.

s0040.literal: He was transferred to General of the Right Army.
s0040.idiomatic: He was promoted to General of the Right Army.

s0041.literal: In the twenty-fourth year of Yuanjia he died, aged sixty-four.
s0041.idiomatic: In the twenty-fourth year of Yuanjia he died, at the age of sixty-four.

s0042.literal: The people of Liang land missed him; on Mount E'gong they raised a temple to sacrifice to him.
s0042.idiomatic: The people of Liang longed for him; on Mount E'gong they raised a temple in his honor.

s0043.literal: In the second year of Shengming he was posthumously made Regular Attendant and Household Minister with the Golden Seal and Purple Cord.
s0043.idiomatic: In the second Shengming year he was posthumously made Regular Attendant and Household Minister with the golden seal and purple cord.

s0044.literal: Xiao Daocheng was born in the fourth year of Yuanjia, the year dingmao.
s0044.idiomatic: Xiao Daocheng was born in the fourth year of Yuanjia, the cyclical year dingmao.

s0045.literal: His bearing and appearance were outstanding; dragon forehead and bell-like voice; scale patterns covered his body.
s0045.idiomatic: His bearing was striking, with a dragon's brow and a bell's resonance; scale-like markings covered his body.

s0046.literal: The scholar Lei Cizong established a school on Cock Cage Mountain; Xiao Daocheng at age thirteen received instruction, studying ritual and the Zuo Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals.
s0046.idiomatic: The scholar Lei Cizong founded a school on Cock Cage Mountain; at thirteen Xiao Daocheng took instruction there in ritual and the Zuo Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals.

s0047.literal: In the seventeenth year, the Song Grand General, Prince of Pengcheng Yikang, was deposed; he garrisoned Yuzhang; the Imperial Father led troops to defend; Xiao Daocheng abandoned his studies and went south.
s0047.idiomatic: In the seventeenth year the Song grand general, Prince Yikang of Pengcheng, was deposed and garrisoned Yuzhang; the Imperial Father led troops to hold the line, and Xiao Daocheng left his studies to go south.

s0048.literal: In the nineteenth year, the Jingling barbarians stirred; Emperor Wen sent Xiao Daocheng at the head of a detached army to attack the barbarians north of the Mian.
s0048.idiomatic: In the nineteenth year the Jingling tribes rose; Emperor Wen sent Xiao Daocheng with a detached force against the barbarians north of the Mian.

s0049.literal: In the twenty-first year, campaigning against the Northern Wei, reaching Mount Qiujian, he together defeated and drove them off.
s0049.idiomatic: In the twenty-first year, on campaign against the Northern Wei, he reached Mount Qiujian and together routed the enemy.

s0050.literal: In the twenty-third year, Yong Province Inspector Xiao Sihua garrisoned Xiangyang and requested that Xiao Daocheng follow him; he garrisoned north of the Mian, attacked the mountain barbarians of Fan and Deng, and broke their settlements.
s0050.idiomatic: In the twenty-third year Yong's inspector Xiao Sihua held Xiangyang and asked that Xiao Daocheng accompany him; he garrisoned north of the Mian, struck the mountain barbarians of Fan and Deng, and destroyed their settlements.

s0051.literal: At first he served as Central Troop Commander in the Left Army.
s0051.idiomatic: His first post was as central corps commander on the Left Army staff.

s0052.literal: In the twenty-seventh year, the Northern Wei besieged Chen Xian, garrison commander of Runan; the court dispatched General Who Pacifies the North Zang Zhi and Chief of Staff for Pacifying the Barbarians Liu Kangzu to rescue him; Emperor Wen sent Xiao Daocheng to proclaim the imperial will and grant overall command.
s0052.idiomatic: In the twenty-seventh year of Yuanjia, the Wei laid siege to Chen Xian at the Runan garrison. The court sent Zang Zhi, General Who Pacifies the North, and Liu Kangzu, chief of staff for the Pacification of the Barbarians, to relieve him. Emperor Wen dispatched Xiao Daocheng to deliver the imperial instructions and invest him with operational authority.

s0053.literal: Hearing that the enemy ruler Tuoba Tao was marching on Pengcheng, Zhi and the others turned the army to rescue; reaching Xuyi, Xiao Daocheng with Zhi's detached army commanders Hu Zongzhi and others—five armies, several thousand infantry and cavalry in the vanguard—Tao had already secretly crossed the Huai; they suddenly met at Mount Guan, joined battle and were defeated, fled along the Huai in retreat, and Zongzhi and the others were all lost.
s0053.idiomatic: When word came that the Wei emperor Tuoba Tao was bearing down on Pengcheng, Zang Zhi and his force wheeled about to relieve the city. At Xuyi, Xiao Daocheng, with Zang Zhi's detached commanders Hu Zongzhi and others—five armies, several thousand foot and horse in the van—found that Tao had already stolen across the Huai. They clashed without warning below Mount Guan, were routed, and fled along the river; Zongzhi and his fellows were swallowed up.

s0054.literal: Xiao Daocheng returned to join Zhi in stubborn defense, was besieged by the enemy, in extreme peril; when affairs were settled, he returned to the capital.
s0054.idiomatic: Xiao Daocheng fell back to hold the line with Zang Zhi. The enemy hemmed them in and the danger was acute; when the crisis passed, he returned to the capital.

s0055.literal: In the twenty-ninth year, he led a detached army to campaign against Chouchi.
s0055.idiomatic: In the twenty-ninth year he took command of a detached force and marched against Chouchi.

s0056.literal: On Liang Province's western border there had long been the Wuxing garrison; in the Long'an era of Jin it was lost and came under the Di.
s0056.idiomatic: Liang Province's western marches had long held the Wuxing garrison, but in Jin's Long'an era it fell to the Di.

s0057.literal: Northwest of Wuxing was the Langao garrison, two hundred li from Chouchi.
s0057.idiomatic: Northwest of Wuxing stood the Langao garrison, two hundred li from Chouchi.

s0058.literal: Xiao Daocheng attacked both fortresses and broke them both.
s0058.idiomatic: Xiao Daocheng stormed both strongholds and took them.

s0059.literal: Then he entered the pass from Gukou; when still eighty li from Chang'an, Liang Province Inspector Liu Xiuzhi sent his army marshal Ma Zhu to assist Xiao Daocheng in attacking Tandi city; they took it, and the enemy's false Prince of Hejian fled.
s0059.idiomatic: He then entered the pass by Gukou. Still eighty li short of Chang'an, Liang Province inspector Liu Xiuzhi sent his marshal Ma Zhu to help Xiao Daocheng take Tandi; the city fell, and the Wei puppet Prince of Hejian ran.

s0060.literal: Enemy relief troops arrived; Xiao Daocheng's army was weary and few; hearing also that Emperor Wen had died, he burned the city and returned to Nanzheng.
s0060.idiomatic: Wei reinforcements arrived while Xiao Daocheng's men were spent and few. When he heard that Emperor Wen had died, he fired the city and withdrew to Nanzheng.

s0061.literal: He inherited the rank of fifth-grade baron of Jinxing County.
s0061.idiomatic: He succeeded to the fifth-rank barony of Jinxing County.

s0062.literal: At the beginning of the Xiaojian era, he was appointed staff officer to the Grand Marshal of the Prince of Jiangxia; when the establishment transferred to Grand Preceptor, he was promoted to outer gentleman, attendant of the Direct Access Office and palace scribe, and [staff officer to the Prince of] Western
s0062.idiomatic: Early in the Xiaojian reign he was named staff officer to the Prince of Jiangxia's grand marshal; when that household became the Grand Preceptor's establishment he went with it, rising to outer court gentleman, attendant in the Direct Access Office, and aide to the Prince of Western

s0064.literal: [Yang] King's military staff officer and magistrate of Jiankang.
s0064.idiomatic: [Yang], as military aide on the prince's staff and magistrate of Jiankang.

s0065.literal: The Prince of Xin'an, Ziluan, enjoyed extraordinary favor; when selecting staff, [Xiao Daocheng] was made Northern
s0065.idiomatic: Prince Ziluan of Xin'an stood in the emperor's highest favor; when the prince chose his staff, Xiao Daocheng was appointed to the Northern

s0067.idiomatic: Army post of central corps commander.

s0068.literal: When Empress Dowager Chen's mourning began, he was recalled to serve as General Who Establishes Martial Glory; he again became magistrate of Jiankang, his central corps command unchanged.
s0068.idiomatic: At the opening of mourning for Empress Dowager Chen he was recalled as General Who Establishes Martial Glory, again made magistrate of Jiankang while retaining his central corps command.

s0069.literal: In the Jinghe era he was appointed General of the Rear Army.
s0069.idiomatic: During the Jinghe reign he was made General of the Rear Army.

s0070.literal: When Emperor Ming acceded, he became General of the Right Army.
s0070.idiomatic: When Emperor Ming took the throne, he was promoted to General of the Right Army.

s0071.literal: At that time the four quarters rebelled; the Administrator of Kuaiji, the Prince of Xunyang Zifang, and the eastern commanderies all raised troops; Emperor Ming added to Xiao Daocheng the title General Who Assists the State and sent him east at the head of an army to attack.
s0071.idiomatic: Rebellion flared on every side. Kuaiji's administrator, Prince Zifang of Xunyang, and the eastern prefectures all took up arms. Emperor Ming gave Xiao Daocheng the rank of General Who Assists the State and sent him east to suppress them.

s0072.literal: Reaching Jinling, he fought the rebels' vanguard generals Cheng Han, Sun Tanwan, and others; in a single day he broke twelve of the enemy camps.
s0072.idiomatic: At Jinling he met the rebel van under Cheng Han, Sun Tanwan, and others and in one day shattered twelve encampments.

s0073.literal: He divided his force to secure the counties; Jinling Administrator Yuan Biao abandoned the city and fled, and the eastern prefectures' cities surrendered one after another.
s0073.idiomatic: He detached columns to pacify the counties. Jinling's administrator Yuan Biao fled his city, and stronghold after stronghold in the east gave way.

s0074.literal: Xuzhou Inspector Xue Andu rebelled at Pengcheng; his nephew Suo'er raided Huaiyin; Shanyang Administrator Cheng Tianzuo rose in the city; Xuzhou Inspector Shen Ling sun also surrendered; Xiao Daocheng was summoned to attack them.
s0074.idiomatic: Xuzhou inspector Xue Andu revolted at Pengcheng. His nephew Suo'er struck at Huaiyin; Shanyang's administrator Cheng Tianzuo turned his city; inspector Shen Lingsun of Xuzhou also went over. Xiao Daocheng was called up to crush them.

s0075.literal: At that time Xiao Daocheng had just pacified the eastern rebels and was about to march south again; he encamped at Xinting, the vanguard already on the road, when Suo'er crossed the Huai from Suiling with more than ten thousand horse and foot, killed the court army commander Sun Geng, and drove his troops against the vanguard Zhang Yong's camp, sending urgent word for help.
s0075.idiomatic: Xiao Daocheng had barely finished in the east and was turning south when he halted at Xinting. His vanguard was already abroad, but Suo'er forded the Huai at Suiling with ten thousand-odd horse and foot, killed the court commander Sun Geng, and pressed Zhang Yong's forward camp, crying for relief.

s0076.literal: Emperor Ming, hearing that the bandits had crossed, urgently recalled Xiao Daocheng to rescue them; he encamped at Pofu.
s0076.idiomatic: When Emperor Ming learned the enemy had crossed the river, he rushed Xiao Daocheng to the rescue. Xiao Daocheng took station at Pofu.

s0077.literal: Suo'er moved on Zhongli; Yong sent General Who Pacifies the North Wang Kuan to hold Xuyi and block his line of retreat.
s0077.idiomatic: Suo'er bore down on Zhongli. Zhang Yong posted Wang Kuan, General Who Pacifies the North, at Xuyi to cut off his retreat.

s0078.literal: Suo'er defeated the court army commander Gao Daoqing, drove him to Shibie, and was about to turn west.
s0078.idiomatic: Suo'er broke the court officer Gao Daoqing and chased him to Shibie, then prepared to march west.

s0079.literal: Wang Kuan and the army commander Ren Nongfu first seized Baihe Stream; Zhang Yong sent Xiao Daocheng at full gallop to oversee Kuan; Suo'er moved east to intercept Xiao Daocheng and keep him from advancing.
s0079.idiomatic: Wang Kuan and the army commander Ren Nongfu seized Baihe Stream first. Zhang Yong sent Xiao Daocheng at the double to supervise Kuan, but Suo'er swung east to bar his path.

s0080.literal: Xiao Daocheng beat the drums, formed ranks, and marched straight into Kuan's camp; Suo'er saw him and did not dare strike.
s0080.idiomatic: Xiao Daocheng beat the drums, dressed his lines, and marched straight into Kuan's camp. Suo'er looked on and did not dare engage.

s0081.literal: After several days Suo'er drew up at Shiliang; Xiao Daocheng pursued him to Gezhong; scouts returned saying the bandits had come; Xiao Daocheng then halted the army and took command, dividing two horse units to wait outside the camp on either flank.
s0081.idiomatic: Several days later Suo'er halted at Shiliang. Xiao Daocheng followed him to Gezhong. When scouts reported the enemy at hand, he halted, took the command in hand, and split two cavalry wings to lie in wait beyond the camp.

s0082.literal: In a little while the enemy's horse and foot closed in together, and they also pushed several lanes of fire-wagons into the fight.
s0082.idiomatic: Presently the rebel horse and foot swarmed in, rolling several lines of fire-carts into the battle.

s0083.literal: They grappled for a long while; then he sent light troops against the enemy's west wing and had the cavalry strike from the rear; the rebel masses were utterly defeated, and in the pursuit their weapons and gear were taken.
s0083.idiomatic: The fight wore on until he sent light troops against their western wing and ordered the horse to close on their rear. The rebel host broke; the pursuit heaped up their arms and baggage.

s0084.literal: He advanced and encamped north of Shiliang Stream.
s0084.idiomatic: He pushed forward and camped north of Shiliang Stream.

s0085.literal: Suo'er sent a thousand men by night to cut the camp; the camp was alarmed; Xiao Daocheng lay and did not rise, ordering those at his side to hold their posts and not move; in a moment the bandits dispersed.
s0085.idiomatic: Suo'er sent a thousand men to raid the camp by night. The lines erupted in alarm, but Xiao Daocheng lay still and gave orders that none should stir from his post; presently the raiders melted away.

s0086.literal: Xiao Daocheng proposed building a fort on the high ground southwest of Shiliang to open a southern road and cut the bandits' escape; Suo'er came as expected to contest it; Xiao Daocheng led the army and broke them, and the enemy horses trampled one another to death.
s0086.idiomatic: Xiao Daocheng planned a fort on the heights southwest of Shiliang to open a road south and sever the enemy's retreat. Suo'er came to dispute the ground as foreseen; Xiao Daocheng led his men and broke him, and the rebel horses stampeded each other to death.

s0087.literal: Suo'er fled toward Zhongli; Xiao Daocheng pursued to the gloaming and returned.
s0087.idiomatic: Suo'er fled toward Zhongli. Xiao Daocheng chased until dark and turned back.

s0088.literal: He was appointed General of Rapid Cavalry, enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiyang County with a fief of six hundred households.
s0088.idiomatic: He was made General of Rapid Cavalry and enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiyang, with a fief of six hundred households.

s0089.literal: He was transferred to army marshal of the Prince of Baling's Guard Army and followed the prince in garrison at Kuaiji.
s0089.idiomatic: He was moved to army marshal on the Prince of Baling's guard staff and went with the prince to garrison Kuaiji.

s0090.literal: Jiang Province Inspector, the Prince of Jin'an Zixun, sent Linchuan Interior Administrator Zhang Yan by the Poyang ridge road into the Three Wu; the court army commander Shen Siren and the false Dragon Rapid General Ren Huang and the false Western Campaign Staff Officer Liu Yuexu each held hazardous ground and faced one another.
s0090.idiomatic: Jiang Province inspector Prince Zixun of Jin'an sent Linchuan's interior administrator Zhang Yan over the Poyang ridge into the Three Wu. The court commander Shen Siren and the rebel generals Ren Huang and Liu Yuexu each held defiles and stood off.

s0091.literal: Emperor Ming sent Xiao Daocheng at the head of three thousand men to attack them.
s0091.idiomatic: Emperor Ming dispatched Xiao Daocheng with three thousand men to bring them to battle.

s0092.literal: At that time the court's armor and weapons had all been committed to the southern campaign; Xiao Daocheng's army was scantily equipped; he therefore plaited palm bark into horse trappings and split bamboo into horse screens; by night he advanced with torches raised, and the bandits, seeing them, were afraid and fled without fighting.
s0092.idiomatic: The court's arms had all gone south, and Xiao Daocheng's column was thinly equipped. He plaited palm bark into horse armor, cut bamboo for cavalry screens, and marched by night with torches lifted. The enemy took fright at the sight and ran before a blow was struck.

s0093.literal: On his return he was appointed army marshal on the Prince of Guiyang's northern campaign staff, Administrator of Southern Donghai, and acting Xuzhou inspector.
s0093.idiomatic: When he returned he was made army marshal on Prince Guiyang's northern campaign staff, administrator of Southern Donghai, and acting inspector of South Xuzhou.

s0094.literal: Earlier, Emperor Ming had sent Zhang Yong and Shen Youzhi with a host to induce Xue Andu to surrender, and said to Xiao Daocheng: "I now mean to use this occasion for a northern campaign—what do you think?"
s0094.idiomatic: Earlier Emperor Ming had sent Zhang Yong and Shen Youzhi with a large force to win Xue Andu over by persuasion. He asked Xiao Daocheng, "I intend to turn this into a northern expedition—what is your view?"

s0095.literal: Xiao Daocheng replied: "Andu lacks talent and insight but has cunning in surplus.
s0095.idiomatic: Xiao Daocheng answered, "Andu is short on ability and judgment but long on guile.

s0096.literal: If you hold the reins long and drive gently, he will surely send his son to court;
s0096.idiomatic: Hold the reins long and drive gently, and he is sure to send his son to court;

s0097.literal: now, if you press him with troops, he will fear and contrive a plan— I fear it will not profit the state."
s0097.idiomatic: but press him now with an army and fear will drive him to scheme. I doubt that will serve the realm."

s0098.literal: The emperor said: "The mass of our armies is fierce and keen—where would they not conquer?
s0098.idiomatic: The emperor said, "Our hosts are fierce and sharp—what place would they not take?

s0099.literal: You lean on your staff at every turn; pray do not say more."
s0099.idiomatic: You lean on your staff and counsel at every turn; for once, say no more."

s0100.literal: When Andu saw the army arrive, he indeed brought in the Northern Wei; Yong and the others were defeated at Pengcheng.
s0100.idiomatic: When Andu saw the army come, he did indeed call in the Wei. Zhang Yong and his fellows were broken at Pengcheng.
